concepts.title: Defining Culture: Wholes and Parts
concepts.definition: Culture is the whole way of life of a people -- learned and shared beliefs, values, norms, language and material objects. Its parts interlock: material culture (tools, dress, buildings) and non-material culture (ideas, customs) change together, so studying one part always implicates the rest.
concepts.key_idea: Culture is the learned and shared design for living -- objects and ideas woven into one whole.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy104.txt lines 15-130 (introduction, defining culture, material and non material culture, culture as way of life, wholeness of culture)
question_patterns: define culture and distinguish its material and non material aspects
in class 11 culture and socialisation: why is culture called a whole way of life
how do the parts of culture interconnect
give examples of material and non material culture
why is culture described as learned and shared
is culture the same as civilisation discuss

solution_steps.explain: Material culture covers tools, dress and buildings; non-material culture covers language, values, beliefs and norms.
A change in objects -- say the smartphone -- pulls ideas and habits along with it; parts move together.
Because it is learned, shared and all-encompassing, culture is best defined as the whole design for living of a people.

worked_examples.q: Ideas and customs form which culture: material or non-material?

concepts.title: Dimensions of Culture: Cognitive, Normative and Beliefs
concepts.definition: Culture works through three dimensions. Cognitive culture is what people know and how they think -- categories, language, knowledge. Normative culture is what they ought to do -- values and norms. Symbolic culture is the meanings attached to things -- a flag, a colour, a gesture -- through which beliefs about the world and the sacred are expressed.
concepts.key_idea: Culture tells you what is (cognition), what ought to be (norms) and what things mean (symbols).
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy104.txt lines 130-250 (dimensions of culture, cognitive and normative components, symbols and beliefs, language as carrier of culture)
question_patterns: explain the cognitive and normative dimensions of culture
in class 11 culture and socialisation: what is the symbolic dimension of culture with examples
how does language carry culture
distinguish values from norms
why are symbols powerful in culture
give an example where the same symbol has different meanings in two cultures

solution_steps.explain: Every culture equips members with categories, concepts and know-how -- what exists and how it works.
Values rank what is desirable; norms convert values into expected conduct with sanctions.
Symbols compress meaning -- gestures, flags, rituals -- and beliefs explain the world, making culture shareable beyond direct experience.

worked_examples.q: Which dimension of culture covers what people know: cognitive or normative?

concepts.title: Socialisation: Becoming a Member of Society
concepts.definition: Socialisation is the lifelong process by which the newborn biological being becomes a social person -- learning language, norms, roles and selfhood through interaction. Primary socialisation in the family forms the basic personality; later phases through school, peers and media continuously resocialise the individual into new roles.
concepts.key_idea: Nobody is born social -- interaction turns the infant into a person, and the process never stops.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy104.txt lines 250-380 (socialisation, agency of the individual, primary and secondary socialisation, agencies family school peer group media)
question_patterns: define socialisation and explain why it is a lifelong process
in class 11 culture and socialisation: what are the agencies of socialisation
distinguish primary socialisation from secondary socialisation
how does the family shape personality
what role do peer groups and media play in socialisation
can socialisation fail discuss cases of isolation

solution_steps.action: follow the infant into the family
solution_steps.explain: Primary socialisation in the closest circle installs language, emotional bonds and basic norms -- the core self.
School, peer groups and media add universalistic norms, competitive roles and new identities -- secondary socialisation.
The individual is not clay: children question, select and even change norms, so socialisation is interactive, not one-way.

worked_examples.q: The lifelong process turning a newborn into a social person is called what?

concepts.title: Identity, Self and the Individual in Society
concepts.definition: The self is socially formed: we come to know who we are through others' expectations and responses, acquiring identities -- gender, caste, nationality, profession -- that position us in society. Individuality and society are not enemies; the distinctive person matures only inside a web of social relationships.
concepts.key_idea: The mirror of society builds the self -- identities are socially given, yet each person assembles them uniquely.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy104.txt lines 380-470 (identity and self, individual and society, socialisation as interactive, modern self and multiple identities)
question_patterns: how does society shape the self and identity
in class 11 culture and socialisation: explain how individuality and society are related
what are social identities give examples
can a person exist outside society discuss
how do others responses build our self image
explain multiple identities of a single individual

solution_steps.explain: Names, gender treatment and expectations arrive before self-awareness, shaping who one takes oneself to be.
Religion, region, language, caste, class and nation supply identities that place the person in society's map.
Society supplies the materials of selfhood; the individual arranges them with agency -- individuality is social, not anti-social.

worked_examples.q: Is the self formed socially or in isolation?

worked_examples.question_pattern: Analyse the celebration of a national festival in terms of the cognitive, normative and symbolic dimensions of culture.

solution_template.explain: Citizens share knowledge of the nation's history and the festival's significance -- what the day commemorates.
Schools and offices close, flags are hoisted -- shared expectations about proper conduct on the day.
The flag, the anthem and the speech stand for the nation itself, condensing belief and feeling into visible signs.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A five-year-old says 'thank you' without being prompted, but a teenager suddenly questions every household rule. Explain both episodes using socialisation.

solution_template.explain: Prompted gratitude has become automatic -- primary socialisation has installed an internalised norm.
The teenager samples peer and public norms, testing the family's rules -- secondary socialisation widening the frame.
Socialisation installs and later re-examines norms; questioning is not its failure but its mature, interactive phase.
